questions.title: Why does a statutory procedural right (5 U.S.C. § 1216) generally fail to satisfy Article III standing without a concrete injury?
questions.question_body: In 'Frazier v. MSPB' and 'Allen v. Wright,' the D.C. Circuit emphasizes that standing requires an 'invasion of a legally protected interest' that is 'concrete and particularized.' In this case, AFL argued they had a 'procedural right' under the Civil Service Reform Act to an OSC investigation. Despite the D.C. Circuit's recognition in cases like 'Ctr. for Law & Educ. v. Dep't of Educ.' that standing standards may be relaxed for procedural injuries, the court here rejected the relaxation. Why was 'OSA's' failure to investigate considered 'procedural right in vacuo' instead of a violation of a right that protects a threatened concrete interest?

questions.title: How does redressability fail when enforcement involves third-party federal agencies like the MSPB and DOJ?
questions.question_body: The opinion describes a redressability chain where OSC would investigate → OSC pursues corrective action (1214/1215) → MSPB sanctions → DOJ produces records. The court cites 'FDA v. All. for Hippocratic Med.' to claim 'causation generally cannot rely on speculation about the unfettered choices made by independent actors.' Does this mean a plaintiff's redressability is inherently more difficult to prove if the potential remedy requires action by a separate administrative board or agency (like the MSPB) that is not a defendant in the suit?

questions.title: Why does an information claim lack standing when the plaintiff cannot demonstrate a statutory entitlement to the information?
questions.question_body: The court distinguishes between 'injury in fact' from an informational perspective and the requirement that the plaintiff be granted information 'that a statute entitled him to receive.' AFL argued they were interested in the 'fruits of the OSC investigation.' However, the court noted OSC could exercise discretion over whether to provide § 1214 notices. Since AFL acknowledges OSC has 'discretion' in § 1216 investigations, why did the court conclude that even § 1216(a)(3)'s mandate to investigate does not create an entitlement to the specific disclosures needed to establish Article III standing?

questions.title: Why did the appellate court vacate for standing rather than decide the district court's specific interpretation of 5 U.S.C. § 1216(a)(3)?
questions.question_body: At the district court level, there was a ruling finding OSC's decision legal error because § 1216(a)(3) 'mandated' such an investigation regardless of § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) predicates. However, the D.C. Circuit declared OSC had discretion under § 1216(c) and vacated the judgment solely for lack of standing. Why did the Court choose to forego deciding the substantive statutory interpretation question, leaving the OSC's actual authority to investigate undiscovered in the face of a successful standing dismissal?
